articles.title: Beauty school moms caught in accreditation crossfire as Trump administration weighs consequential decision
articles.summary: Trump's Department of Education faces a pivotal decision on NACCAS accreditation that could cut federal student aid for 120,000 beauty students.
articles.body: The Trump administration is weighing the future of an accreditor overseeing roughly 1,300 beauty and cosmetology schools and more than 120,000 students, in a decision that could test how the president’s push to overhaul higher education accreditation is applied beyond the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) battles that have dominated the issue. President Donald Trump promised during the 2024 campaign to "fire the radical left accreditors" and called accreditation his "secret weapon" against colleges and universities he argued had been captured by the political left. But the case now before the U.S. Department of Education (DOE) is different. Rather than allegations involving DEI requirements, it centers on whether the National Accrediting Commission of Career Arts and Sciences, or NACCAS, has complied with federal requirements and what consequences should follow if it has not. MCMAHON TELLS HOUSE PANEL TRUMP ADMIN MOVING TO DISMANTLE ‘FAILED’ $3T EDUCATION BUREAUCRACY That distinction matters to students because recognition by a DOE-approved accreditor is generally necessary for schools to participate in federal student aid programs. NACCAS says it accredits approximately 1,300 institutions serving more than 120,000 students in cosmetology, beauty and related career programs. DOE staff identified deficiencies with NACCAS but recommended continuing its federal recognition with restrictions, additional reporting and monitoring while it works to come into compliance. The National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity, or NACIQI, took a harder line at its July meeting, voting 9-3 to recommend that the department deny NACCAS renewed recognition. TRUMP ADMIN TIGHTENS VISE ON STUDENT AID FRAUD IN ‘GHOST STUDENT’ CRACKDOWN The DOE has not made a final decision. The Department of Education told Fox News Digital that accreditor recognition is reviewed every five years through a three-step process: DOE staff makes a recommendation; the independent bipartisan NACIQI makes its own recommendation; a senior department official makes the final judgment based on both. "We will not comment on details as the process is ongoing," the DOE said. For some students, the federal process has raised concerns about a source of funding they say they could not have attended beauty school without. TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES Aliyah Fernandez, a recent Hollywood Institute cosmetology graduate and mother who now works as an assistant in a salon, said federal aid made her education possible. "I could not have afforded beauty school without federal financial aid," Fernandez told Fox News Digital. "It was because of that that I could attend at all." Fernandez said she chose cosmetology in part because she wanted a career that would allow her to earn a living while remaining present in her daughter's life. "I knew that if I worked full-time 9 to 5, I wouldn't barely have any time to see her grow up," Fernandez said. "I really just wanted to be there for her. "I wanted an opportunity to financially support her and be present in her life at the same time," she added. "I wanted to have both." I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT; TRUMP IS RIGHT TO MAKE COLLEGES DELIVER FOR STUDENTS Blythe Fields, an expectant mother who is studying cosmetology while working in salons, said she previously paid for esthetician school herself and spent roughly two years saving her tips to continue her education. "I paid out of pocket for esthetician school, and it made me go broke," Fields told Fox News Digital. Fields said she now works during the day and attends school at night, describing her schedule as "literally 12-hour days." She said federal financial aid allowed her to continue her education and that the flexibility of cosmetology will become even more important when her baby arrives. "The first year is so important, and I need to be able to have that flexibility to raise a child," she said. Fernandez and Fields both said they helped start a petition asking the DOE not to adopt NACIQI's recommendation outright. The petition calls instead for a monitored improvement period that would allow NACCAS to address the government's findings while maintaining recognition. Fernandez said she understood why federal officials raised concerns about NACCAS but believed denying recognition would go too far. FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING "Having done the research myself, I can completely understand, you know, the side of the board," Fernandez said. "However, I do not think a full termination of accreditation is reasonable considering how many people rely on this." Fields was more pointed when asked what she would tell Trump before his administration makes the final decision. "I would ask him who cuts and colors his hair and how did they get there?" Fields said. The disagreement over NACCAS centers on whether the deficiencies identified during its federal review warrant continued oversight or denial of recognition. Education Department staff recommended that NACCAS be prohibited from accrediting additional institutions until it demonstrates compliance, complete corrective action within 12 months and submits additional reports to the department. NACIQI instead recommended denial. Zakiya Smith Ellis, a former Obama administration DOE official who serves on the advisory committee, made the motion to deny NACCAS renewed recognition. Michael Poliakoff seconded the motion, which passed 9-3. Smith Ellis argued during the July meeting that NACCAS had been given opportunities to address compliance problems and questioned whether giving it additional time would be sufficient. She also raised concerns about debt and earnings among students at NACCAS-accredited institutions. Three committee members voted against denial, including Robert Eitel, who served in the DOE during Trump's first term. Eitel argued that NACCAS should be required to correct its deficiencies rather than lose recognition and raised concerns about the potential consequences for the schools and students it oversees. The proceeding also creates an unusual contrast with the accreditation practices Trump highlighted in his April executive order. The order directed the DOE to investigate whether accreditors require schools to engage in unlawful discrimination, including through DEI-related standards. The federal findings at issue in the NACCAS proceeding concern compliance and oversight rather than an allegation that NACCAS imposes DEI requirements. Smith Ellis, meanwhile, has publicly defended DEI policies and previously served as a senior DOE official during the Obama administration. Fox News Digital asked Smith Ellis why she favored denying recognition rather than the corrective measures recommended by DOE staff and what she would say to students concerned about the potential consequences. Smith Ellis did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Fields told Fox News Digital she believes beauty careers can be overlooked in ways that other skilled trades are not. Asked whether she thought the same fight would be playing out around traditionally male-dominated trades such as plumbing or welding, she said she did not. They just think, ‘Oh, they went to hair school. It's easy.’" For Fields, however, the training will give her the career she hopes will allow her to earn a living while raising her child.The White House, NACCAS, and the Hollywood Institute of Beauty did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Former President George W. Bush, who was in office on Sept. 11, 2001, will give remarks Wednesday to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.

In the aftermath of the tragic events, Bush created the Department of Homeland Security in 2002 to tackle future threats.

The ex-president will be speaking with his former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice from his presidential center at Southern Methodist University in Dallas.

He is also expected to attend the ceremony Friday at Ground Zero alongside former Presidents Obama, Biden and Clinton and Vice President Vance. President Trump will give remarks at the Pentagon.

articles.body:
Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas) said Wednesday that Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) must debate his opponent, Democratic nominee James Talarico, to win the state’s Senate election.

In an interview with Nexstar, which owns The Hill, Sessions was asked whether he supported Paxton’s bid for Senate.

“Of course I do,” the lawmaker said. “He’s running for a competitive position, he’s going to have to be judged on how well he defends himself, his ideas and then be seen on stage vis-à-vis his opponent. That is how you win.”

Answering a follow-up question, Sessions said: “Well, I don’t think he can win without the debate. About 30 percent of the electorate is looking for this to be done.

“They would expect it to be done, and they would expect him to define himself, to stand up for what he believes in, to take the shots at him, and to be able to effectively show the difference between the two candidates. I don’t think there’s any question about that.”

Talarico has repeatedly bashed Paxton for not appearing in debates with him.

“I agreed to 3 debates over a month ago. You declined every single one. You love to talk tough on Fox. Say it to me on the debate stage,” he said in August in a post on social platform X.

Despite having President Trump’s endorsement, Paxton trailed Talarico by 6 points in an August poll from Texas Public Opinion Research.

Paxton has faced several notable scandals, including the Texas state House voting to impeach him on corruption charges — of which the state Senate later acquitted him.

If elected, Talarico would be the first Democrat to win a Texas statewide election in more than three decades.

articles.title: Potential Dem presidential contender crashes GOP convention, tries to snatch spotlight from Trump
articles.summary: Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker claims Republicans are trying to "rig" the 2026 midterm elections as the GOP kicks off its first-ever convention in Dallas.
articles.body: DALLAS — Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois is urging voters to ignore the Republicans' first-ever midterm convention. "Voters can see through the BS that Republicans are spewing," Pritzker told reporters at a Democratic National Committee-hosted counter programming news conference across the street from the American Airlines Center in Dallas, the site of this week’s first-ever Republican midterm convention. With less than two months until the midterm elections — and early voting just weeks away — President Donald Trump and the GOP kicked off their convention Wednesday as Republicans fight to keep control of Congress. The GOP's playbook for the convention, which comes as Republicans face energized Democrats and political headwinds as they defend their slim House and Senate majorities, is to motivate the party's base and boost turnout in key races that will determine control of Congress. GOP MIDTERM CONVENTION: CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? "We are putting the president on the ballot," Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters emphasized in a Fox News Digital interview on the eve of the gathering. "That's exactly what we're doing with this midterm convention." But Pritzker, a potential 2028 White House contender, blasted the two-day GOP confab. "This bizarre Republican midterm convention here can't paper over the fact that Republicans have done nothing to earn your vote," Pritzker said. "Donald Trump is hoping that a flashy primetime event will make you forget that, well, his trade war is killing costs for families at the grocery store. His war in Iran is killing ranchers and farmers and their way of life, and his war on people, on the working people, the working families of this country are raising the costs of health care and housing." FIRST ON FOX: WHO'S SPEAKING — AND WHEN — AT THE GOP'S HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION The governor also charged that Republicans are trying to "rig" the midterm elections, arguing that Trump is aiming to use the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail-in balloting across the country. "Republicans know that they can't win on the merits of their unpopular policies. So, they're working to rig the 2026 election," Pritzker charged. Pritzker also warned that "if Democrats don’t win, if they don’t win in this election, we may not have other elections, or certainly we’re going to have future elections, every single one of which will be rigged." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB The White House has defended Trump's executive order on mail-in voting as a "commonsense measure" aimed at ensuring secure elections. Pritzker, who is running for re-election this year for a third term steering Democrat-dominated Illinois, is seen as a possible presidential contender in the 2028 White House race to succeed Trump. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the governor pivoted when asked by Fox News if his stop in Dallas should be seen as a 2028 signal. Standing alongside some top Texas Democrats, Pritzker said, "I care a great deal about what happens in Texas. Voters everywhere in the country should care about what happens in Texas. So, I'm pleased to be here for that reason. If I can advance the cause, that's why I should stand here."

articles.title: House GOP leaders use convention speeches to take aim at ‘crazy communists’
articles.summary: House Republican leaders are sharpening their attacks on Democratic progressives and socialists as the party looks to hold its narrow majority, using the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, to frame the 2026 midterms as an existential fight for the country. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) said Wednesday in remarks to the crowd at…
articles.body:
House Republican leaders are sharpening their attacks on Democratic progressives and socialists as the party looks to hold its narrow majority, using the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, to frame the 2026 midterms as an existential fight for the country.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) said Wednesday in remarks to the crowd at the convention that “this is not your father’s Democrat party.”

“The Democrat Party has been completely taken over by crazy communists. I call it the Bolshevik Revolution in the Democrat Party. And if they get back the gavel, let me tell you what they will do. You know what they will do. The first thing they do is impeach President Trump and his cabinet. … They will repeal no tax on overtime, no tax on tips. They said they’ll raise taxes on every hardworking American,” Scalise said.

He added that the midterms are a contrast between “common sense versus crazy communists” and urged Republicans to turn up in November.

“Show up and vote Republican up and down the ballot. President Trump’s America First agenda is at stake,” he said.

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) echoed similar sentiments, accusing Democrats of having “no leader” and “no message.”

“The only thing they can agree on is their disgusting hatred of America and our great president. These people are sick …There is absolutely nothing democratic about socialism. By the way, these people aren’t even socialists. They’re communists and they’re anarchists and they hate our country,” Emmer said.

Their remarks come as Democratic progressives and socialists have scored a string of primary victories in the past few months, giving Republicans fresh fodder for their midterm message. GOP leaders have argued that recent victories by candidates they describe as “insurgent” could pull the country too far to the left.

They have also warned that their political opponents would back tax hikes and massive reparations, seize private property and businesses, and lead the country to communism — at a time when many Americans are already struggling to make ends meet.

“To the American people listening, I say, if all you want out of life is what little these communists are offering, I guess that’s your right. Or you can join Donald J. Trump and Republicans, and have the opportunity to realize your greatest dreams, to achieve your greatest potential, to live free in the greatest country the world has ever known,” Emmer said.

Decision Desk HQ forecast in July that Democrats are favored to win back the House, while the Senate is on track to hold a 50-50 partisan split.

articles.body:
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) appeared in a video praising Sen. Dave McCormick (Pa.) at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention Wednesday.

“Why am I here talking to you today?” Fetterman said in a pre-recorded video. “Because, well, I’m a common sense Democrat.”

“David McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done” he added, noting the duo would work with President Trump to help revitalize Pennsylvania’s manufacturing industry while calling McCormick a “friend.”

Manufacturing jobs in the commonwealth have declined slightly during the president’s second term, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data analyzed by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

Earlier this summer. Fetterman and McCormick teamed up to launch a joint fundraising committee.

Fetterman also said in the video that he would always “reject the extremes in socialism and that anti-American way of life” — comments that come as democratic socialist and progressive candidates have won their Democratic primaries for Senate and House.

Fetterman has attracted the ire of many of his Democratic colleagues in both chambers for breaking with the party on multiple issues. The Pennsylvania senator has notably been the only Democrat to vote against every Senate war powers resolution seeking to force Trump to wind down the Iran war.

Fetterman, a staunch supporter of Israel, has vocally supported the U.S. operation against the Islamic Republic on social media and during TV interviews — including on Fox News.

Last year, Fetterman voted in line with Trump’s position 28 percent of the time, the most of any Senate Democrat, per data from VoteHub . The Democratic lawmaker was among a small group of Democrats to join Republicans in voting to end the record-long government shutdown last November.

The Pennsylvania senator has said he has no plans to become a Republican, but he laid out his red line for departing the Democratic Party in July

“If our party ever becomes — and just makes it official — the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave,” he told The Hill’s Alexander Bolton at the Hill Nation Summit.

Criticism of Fetterman ramped up among his Democratic colleagues over the weekend, after The Wall Street Journal published a story outlining the senator’s alleged lack of commitment to his duties.

Fetterman pushed back on the report, telling CNN his former “disgruntled staffers” are promoting “smears” about him.

articles.title: Sen. John Fetterman makes a surprise cameo praising Republicans at the GOP convention
articles.summary: The Democratic senator appeared on video promoting the efforts of President Donald Trump and Sen. Dave McCormick in shaping the U.S. Steel deal with Nippon Steel.
articles.body: DALLAS — Just eight weeks out from the midterm elections, Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., gave Republicans a boost on Wednesday night. Fetterman appeared on video at the Republican midterm convention, praising Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., and touting working with President Donald Trump. “Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a common-sense Democrat,” Fetterman said in the video message. “I’m always going to stand with America. I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and the anti-American way of life. Dave McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done, and he’s going to fight for Pennsylvania. I’m proud to count him as my friend.” Fetterman also pointed to a U.S. Steel mill behind him, saying, “That’s exactly the kind of thing that we’ll work together, and we’ll work with President Trump, to fight and defend the steel way of life, right here in the Steel Valley.” McCormick then thanked Fetterman for his “friendship” and his “courage.” Reaction in the convention hall was muted for Fetterman’s message, with only a few attendees cheering. The crowd did give a loud applause when Fetterman concluded his message to introduce McCormick on stage. The appearance comes as Fetterman has built a close bipartisan relationship with McCormick. The two even launched a joint fundraising committee together, which triggered a wave of Democratic criticism of Fetterman, who has toyed with leaving the party but has vowed not to. Former Fetterman aides who spoke with NBC News on Wednesday said the Democratic senator’s decision to appear at an event — nicknamed “Trumpapalooza” — to boost Republicans ahead of the critical midterm elections was beyond the pale. One former aide to the senator described the appearance as “pathetic” and said McCormick is “working him like dog.” “He is a troll so this kind of behavior makes sense, but to see it executed at this scale is really stunning,” Trè Easton, a former legislative aide to Fetterman, said. “Also in what world is bear-hugging Trump, who is sitting at 27% approval in the state, smart for anyone? Obviously dumb for a Democrat to do it. But even if he’s thinking of going independent or fully switching, I just don’t think it rebounds to his benefit long term.” One former top Fetterman aide, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the relationship, told NBC News last month that the senator has referred to McCormick as “his mentor” and seeks his approval. This person said the pair often text one another and have dinner back in Pennsylvania. Both live in the Pittsburgh area. The appearance followed a bombshell report in The Wall Street Journal in which former aides to the senator provided texts and internal documents detailing Fetterman’s lack of interest in engaging with constituents. After that story published, McCormick came to Fetterman’s aid. “These stories are the latest example of outrageously disloyal staff and forces on the Left using anonymous leaks to cancel my friend John Fetterman,” he wrote on X. “They hate that he is an independent thinker who refuses to fall into line so they want to silence him.”

articles.title: Illegal alien ordered removed years ago charged in crash that killed newly engaged 23-year-old teacher
articles.summary: Cameron Lyon, a newly engaged Ohio teacher, was killed when a previously deported illegal immigrant allegedly flipped his SUV into oncoming traffic.
articles.body: A previously deported illegal alien allegedly drove drunk before flipping his SUV into oncoming traffic and killing a newly engaged Ohio teacher, authorities said. Alvaro Uribe-Gonzalez, a 33-year-old Mexican national who federal officials say illegally returned to the U.S. after being deported, now faces aggravated vehicular homicide and other charges in the death of 23-year-old Cameron Lyon. Lyon’s fiancée, 23-year-old Abrielle Kerns, was seriously injured in the fiery Sunday evening crash on U.S. Route 33 in Fairfield County, according to her family. The Ohio State Highway Patrol initially described Kerns’ injuries as non-life-threatening, but relatives said she remained in intensive care "fighting to recover" as the family grappled with Lyon’s death. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECT CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED POLICE OFFICER AND HIS GIRLFRIEND "This is an unconscionable tragedy because it was preventable," Republican Ohio gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy wrote. "This perpetrator shouldn’t have ever been in our country, let alone permitted to remain here." Ramaswamy pointed to Uribe-Gonzalez’s alleged drunken driving and immigration history as he vowed to take action if elected governor. "But he ended up driving drunk & killed an innocent young man in Ohio. I won’t tolerate this in our state," Ramaswamy wrote. "So devastating. It doesn’t have to be this way. I’ll fix it in Ohio next year & will go hard as necessary." The Ohio State Highway Patrol said Lyon was driving west when Uribe-Gonzalez’s eastbound GMC Terrain went off the right side of the highway shortly after 6 p.m. DAD OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DUI VICTIM ISSUES WARNING TO AMERICANS OVER LAX DRIVER'S LICENSE LAWS Uribe-Gonzalez allegedly overcorrected, veered across the roadway and overturned into the westbound lanes, slamming into Lyon’s Chevrolet Trax. The GMC then caught fire. Lyon was treated at the crash site but died a short time later, the patrol said. Uribe-Gonzalez suffered minor injuries. Investigators said alcohol is suspected to have played a role in the crash. Uribe-Gonzalez was charged with aggravated vehicular homicide, driving under the influence of alcohol and operating a motor vehicle without a valid license. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer with the Fairfield County Jail the day after his arrest, asking local officials not to release him before federal agents can take custody. ILLEGAL ALIEN CHARGED WITH KILLING 4 YOUNG PEOPLE IN WRONG-WAY DUI CRASH ON OKLAHOMA HIGHWAY The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said Uribe-Gonzalez first entered the country illegally through Texas in January 2020 and was arrested by Border Patrol. An immigration judge issued a final removal order Jan. 11, 2020, and the Trump administration deported him to Mexico April 14 of that year, according to DHS. Federal officials said Uribe-Gonzalez later illegally crossed back into the U.S. at an unknown date and location. "This illegal alien has been charged with aggravated vehicular homicide and driving under the influence of alcohol after allegedly causing a car crash that killed 23-year-old Cameron Lyon in Ohio," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. ICE URGES NORTH CAROLINA TO KEEP ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN TRIPLE-FATAL HIT-AND-RUN BEHIND BARS "Cameron had his whole life ahead of him, and that life was stolen by this criminal who never should have been in our country in the first place." Mullin said ICE wants Ohio officials to cooperate with the detainer so Uribe-Gonzalez can be taken into federal custody and removed from the country. Lyon had recently begun his first teaching job and was well-loved by staff and students at Crestline Exempted Schools, according to a fundraiser for his family. A graduate of Otterbein University, Lyon was remembered as a cherished son, brother and friend whose death left his family and community devastated. THREE-TIME DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH KILLING NORTH CAROLINA GIRL, 6, AFTER RUNNING STOP SIGN Lyon and Kerns had recently become engaged and were preparing to begin their life together. The couple had moved into a home that had been in Lyon’s family for generations and were renovating it together, according to Earthly Pottery Co., where Kerns worked. "We are devastated by this needless tragedy and miss him dearly," organizers of the fundraiser for Lyon’s family wrote. A separate fundraiser organized by Kerns’ aunt and uncle said the family was standing beside her through the "shock, pain and uncertainty" of the difficult days following the crash. "Everyone who knew Abrielle and Cameron could see the love they shared and the future they were building together," the family wrote. ILLEGAL ALIEN ACCUSED OF KILLING DAD, TRYING TO FLEE AFTER DRUNKEN CRASH – FEDS RIP BIDEN-ERA RELEASE The money raised will help cover Kerns’ medical bills and the mounting challenges she faces as she recovers and begins rebuilding her life without Lyon. "Her world has been turned upside down, and the physical and emotional hardships ahead will be enormous," organizers wrote. The tragedy has rippled through the community as local businesses rallied around Kerns and Lyon’s family. Millersport Coffee announced it will donate a portion of its weekend sales to support Lyon’s family and help cover Kerns’ medical needs. "The entire Kerns family is like family to us," the coffee shop wrote. "We are incredibly thankful that she survived, while we grieve with her and the Lyon family over the heartbreaking loss of her fiancé, Cameron Lyon." ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO KILLED NASHVILLE RESTAURANT OWNER TO FACE ICE DEPORTATION AFTER PRISON Earthly Pottery Co. said Kerns had helped teach its classes, while Lyon was always willing to lend a hand when the business needed help. "Their little lives were taking shape and we got a front row seat," the business wrote. "We were texting earlier in the day about getting her studio all set up." "A family has lost a son, a brother, a classroom has lost their teacher, friends have lost their friend," Earthly Pottery Co. wrote. The crash remains under investigation.

articles.title: Businesswoman Helena Foulkes defeats Gov. Daniel McKee in Rhode Island Democratic governor primary
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Foulkes won the Democratic nomination in the blue state, making McKee the first governor to fall in a primary in eight years.
articles.body: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee has lost his Democratic primary to former CVS executive Helena Foulkes, NBC News projects, after having faced a significant spending disadvantage and voter discontent with his tenure. In an election season that has seen a wave of anti-incumbent energy, McKee, 75, becomes the first governor to fall in a primary this year — and the first in eight years. Public polling had shown McKee, who was running for a full second term, trailing by double digits heading into Tuesday. And Foulkes, 62, outspent him on the airwaves by 3-to-1, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. The primary was a rematch of 2022, when Foulkes narrowly lost to McKee, who had replaced Gov. Gina Raimaondo after she was selected for President Joe Biden’s Cabinet in 2021. McKee’s 2023 decision to close the Washington Bridge, a commuter thoroughfare in Providence, hung over his campaign. The bridge closure came after state engineers discovered major structural problems that could have eventually caused it to collapse. Three years later, the bridge remains under construction. An Emerson College poll in August found that 63% of likely Rhode Island voters disapproved of McKee’s handling of the Washington Bridge, with just 18% saying they approved. In her campaign ads, Foulkes said the state had “the worst roads and bridges.” She also touted her plans to boost the state’s economy and housing market. McKee has defended his decision to close the bridge, saying he prioritized safety over politics, and he has said construction will be completed by 2028. The last time a sitting governor lost a primary was in 2018, when Kansas Republican Jeff Colyer was defeated by then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump. Hawaii’s Neil Abercrombie was the last Democratic governor to fall in a primary, losing by 35 points to David Ige, who was a state senator at the time, in 2014. Eleven House members and two senators have lost primaries this year. Given the heavy focus on local issues, the Rhode Island primary did not attract the level of national attention other Democratic contests around the country — which centered on fierce ideological and generational battles — have attracted this year. Still, Foulkes does have connections to powerful Democrats. Thomas Dodd and Chris Dodd, her uncle and grandfather, were both U.S. senators from Connecticut. And former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who was a college roommate of Foulkes’ mother, campaigned for her. Foulkes will be the heavy favorite in the general election in the blue state, which has not elected a Republican governor since 2010. Kamala Harris carried it by nearly 14 points in the 2024 presidential election.

articles.body:
Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee is projected to lose his reelection bid to former CVS executive Helena Foulkes in the Democratic primary for Rhode Island, according to Decision Desk HQ. (DDHQ).

Foulkes led McKee by nearly 25 percentage points — 62 percent to nearly 38 percent — per DDHQ.

It’s the second time the pair have faced off against each other for Rhode Island’s Democratic primary for governor. McKee narrowly beat Foulkes in the 2022 primary.

The governor, who’s served in the role since 2021 after former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo was tapped to join the Biden administration, faced intense scrutiny and frustration over his administration’s handling of the closure and rebuilding of the state’s Washington Bridge.

The bridge, which ran from Providence to East Providence, was closed in 2023 after engineers spotted defects that they worried could cause the infrastructure to collapse.

The governor has defended his administration’s handling of the bridge closure, pointing out that the demolition finished earlier than expected. His administration says the bridge is expected to reopen by 2028.

Polling heading into the Democratic primary suggested that his response may not have been enough to placate voters, with Foulkes leading the incumbent.

McKee, meanwhile, attacked Foulkes over CVS and its ties to the opioid epidemic. The company reached a settlement in 2022 that agrees to pay about $5 billion to states in litigation related to the opioid crisis.

Foulkes has suggested that the retailer cracked down hard against “pill mill” doctors and that there was an “almost 40 percent reduction in opioids” during her tenure.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Rhode Island governor’s seat “solid Democrat,” making Foulkes the favorite to win in November.

articles.body:
Sen. Jack Reed (D) sailed through his Rhode Island Democratic primary on Wednesday, easily besting longshot challengers, according to a Decision Desk HQ projection.

The win in the deep blue state puts the 76-year-old incumbent on a glidepath to win a sixth term in the Senate.

Reed defeated progressive Connor Burbridge, a 31-year-old eldercare worker and Army veteran who argued it was high time for a change in leadership, and Luis Daniel Muñoz, a 41-year-old consultant and former candidate for governor. He led Burbridge by about 60 percentage points nearly 50 percent of the vote reported per DDHQ.

Rhode Island’s House and Senate seats have all been steadily blue for decades, and Democrats have held the governor’s mansion since 2014.

Together with three terms in the House, Reed has served on Capitol Hill for more than three decades. An Army veteran, he’s the ranking member of the Senate’s Armed Services Committee.

Rhode Island is the second-to-last primary of the 2026 midterm cycle, before Delaware’s primaries next Tuesday close out the calendar and kickstart the run-up to November’s general election.

articles.title: US states sue Trump over weakening of endangered species protections
articles.summary: Attorneys general from 20 states and Washington, DC, say the US government illegally rolled back landmark protections.
articles.body:
A group of attorneys general in the United States have sued President Donald Trump’s administration for weakening protections for endangered species .

The group of 20 Democratic-led states, plus the District of Columbia, filed two lawsuits on Wednesday.

The complaints come less than two months after the Department of Interior and Department of Commerce announced final rules that could make it easier for companies to develop sensitive lands that are home to endangered species.

“The Trump administration is trying to undermine the law, the will of Congress and the will of the people who overwhelmingly support protections for endangered species,” Washington state Attorney General Nick Brown said at a news conference.

“Instead of stewardship, this administration’s approach to our land, to our water, is one of exploitation.”

One of the two lawsuits argues that the government has unlawfully narrowed the definition of “harm” in the 1973 Endangered Species Act, a landmark piece of legislation to protect animals and plants at risk of extinction.

“Harm”, under the law, has long been interpreted to include threats to those species’ habitats.

But the Trump administration’s new rule marks a “reversal of staggering proportions”, the states argued.

It would open the door to activities such as mining and oil drilling in sensitive habitats so long as they are not “directed immediately and intentionally” at particular animals.

Environmental groups have also sued over the change.

The second lawsuit filed on Wednesday challenges two new rules. One eliminates wide protections for newly-threatened species unless the US Fish and Wildlife Service creates species-specific regulations.

The second rule requires the government to consider objections from private companies before declaring areas “critical habitats”.

The lawsuit argues that such changes leave endangered species with fewer safeguards than what Congress had outlined in its law.

The 1973 law has been credited with helping restore the populations of animals such as condors, grizzly bears and humpback whales. It is seen as a keystone achievement of US conservation efforts.

But the Trump administration has pledged to roll back environmental protections in favour of prioritising economic growth.

“Drill, baby, drill” was a popular slogan during Trump’s 2024 re-election campaign, as he promised to open protected lands to greater oil exploration and private development.

Critics of Trump’s regulation-slashing fear he may trigger irreversible changes, pushing species to extinction.

“Caring for our wildlife and our environment is part of caring for our future,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement. “Yet President Trump seems to care only for himself and his industry friends.”

But the Trump administration has argued that environmental protections have gone too far.

It accused Wednesday’s lawsuits of seeking to defend “regulatory overreach” that went beyond what Congress had intended.

“The role of federal agencies is to faithfully implement the Endangered Species Act as written, not to expand its reach through interpretations favoured by advocacy organizations,” an Interior Department spokesperson said, according to the Reuters news agency.

articles.title: Incumbents fall in Rhode Island primaries: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: It was a bad night to be an incumbent in Rhode Island on Wednesday, with the governor and the mayor of the state’s largest city losing their Democratic primaries. Former CVS executive Helena Foulkes defeated Democratic Gov. Dan McKee while Providence Mayor Brett Smiley lost to democratic socialist state Rep. David Morales. Though McKee’s primary focused more on voter dissatisfaction over…
articles.body:
It was a bad night to be an incumbent in Rhode Island on Wednesday, with the governor and the mayor of the state’s largest city losing their Democratic primaries.

Former CVS executive Helena Foulkes defeated Democratic Gov. Dan McKee while Providence Mayor Brett Smiley lost to democratic socialist state Rep. David Morales.

Though McKee’s primary focused more on voter dissatisfaction over his handling of the closure and reconstruction of a major bridge in the Ocean State, Wednesday’s results underscore the anti-establishment energy surging in contests across the country this cycle.

Sen. Jack Reed easily won the Democratic nomination for a sixth term in the upper chamber.

That leaves Delaware as the lone state left to hold its primaries next week before all eyes turn toward the general election this fall.

Here are three takeaways from Wednesday’s primaries in Rhode Island:

Sitting governor loses primary for first time since 2018

McKee is the first governor to lose a primary in recent memory.

The last time was in 2018, when former Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer, who had ascended to the governor’s mansion when former Gov. Sam Brownback (R) resigned to join the Trump administration as an ambassador in 2018, lost his bid for a full term that year.

Former Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie (D), meanwhile, is the last elected incumbent to unsuccessfully seek his party nomination. He lost in 2014.

Foulkes defeated the incumbent by 25 percentage points as of 9 p.m. EDT Wednesday, with 84 percent of the vote recorded.

Mckee’s loss isn’t particularly surprising, however. Foulkes held a 15-point lead over McKee in the latest Emerson College polling.

McKee and Foulkes first faced off against each other in 2022, with the governor edging out his opponent by just shy of 3 percentage points in the primary. On the campaign trail, the incumbent aought to attack Foulkes over her role at CVS amid the opioid crisis.

Testament to the fact that all politics is local, the Rhode Island governor’s downfall centered in large part on the state’s slow pace fixing a key piece of infrastructure.

McKee had drawn the ire of Rhode Islanders over the closure of the westbound Washington Bridge for years. The bridge, which connects Providence to East Providence, has been closed since 2023 and isn’t expected to be completed until November 2028.

Demolition of the bridge finished in December — which McKee’s administration points out was ahead of schedule — after the state closed the throughway due to structural issues three years prior.

“I know there is a lot of frustration, and I accept it,” McKee told The New York Times in a recent interview. “But in the end, people are going to realize we did the right thing.”

Still, the closure of the westbound bridge added lengthier commutes for residents and created an economic toll on key industries like the hospitality sector.

“We’re not just talking about the Washington Bridge, we’re talking about a culture here where a few guys at the top know what’s going on, and the rest of us are in the dark,” Foulkes said during a gubernatorial debate against McKee last month, according to the Rhode Island Current.

Democratic socialists notch win in Providence

Rhode Island state Rep. David Morales defeated Smiley in Wednesday’s primary, marking another win for the Democratic Party’s left flank this primary cycle.

As of 9 p.m. EDT Wednesday, Morales led Smiley by 6 points in the vote returns.

Democratic socialists have dominated conversation this primary season — and the surging energy on the far-left shows no signs of waning. Several democratic socialists are on track to win House elections in November, while two notched the Democratic nomination for Senate in Florida and Oklahoma.

Morales’s victory over Smiley adds another socialist to the mayoral ranks across the country. Morales is expected to easily win his general election in the blue state.

Both Seattle and New York City are led by democratic socialists, Katie Wilson and Zohran Mamdani, respectively.

Meanwhile, democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George in Washington, D.C. is on the fast track to succeed outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser in November. Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is challenging Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass too.

articles.title: Trump gave aide Natalie Harp a $45,000 holiday cash gift, disclosure shows
articles.summary: Federal employees are generally barred from receiving compensation beyond their government salaries.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump gave tens of thousands of dollars in cash gifts last year to four White House aides, raising questions about whether he violated federal ethics rules governing compensation for government employees.

Executive assistant Natalie Harp, communications adviser Margo Martin and deputy director of Oval Office operations Chamberlain Harris each received $45,000, according to financial disclosures released by the administration last week.

Meanwhile, Walt Nauta, the director of Oval Office operations, received $20,000. The money was labelled as “Cash Gift for Holidays”.

Federal employees are generally barred from receiving compensation beyond their government salaries, raising questions over whether the payments are permissible. The White House, however, said the gifts complied with ethics rules.

“The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said.

Ingle added that Trump has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his “orbit”, both during his time in government and in the private sector.

The $45,000 payments were equivalent to roughly one-third of the annual salaries Harp, Martin and Harris received. They are paid $150,000 a year. Nauta’s annual compensation is $175,000.

Harp and Nauta are among Trump’s closest aides, with near-constant access to the president at the White House and while travelling.

Harp, for instance, helps manage Trump’s Truth Social account and drafts social media statements, according to a person familiar with her role.

She is also known for carrying a portable printer that provides Trump with news coverage, earning her the nickname the “human printer”.

Her close relationship with the president has made her the subject of public scrutiny in recent months. At one midterm rally, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff questioned Trump’s commitment to public service, pointing to his travels with Harp.

“He doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie,” Ossoff said.

Trump has cultivated a similarly tight bond with Nauta. A former White House valet, Nauta continued to work for Trump after he lost re-election in 2020, taking on roles at the president’s Mar-a-Lago resort and within his political action committee.

He has since returned to the White House as part of Trump’s second administration.

Between Trump’s two terms, however, Nauta was a co-defendant, alongside Trump, in a federal indictment alleging the Republican leader illegally withheld classified documents outside of office.

Nauta was charged with conspiring to conceal the documents and obstruct the federal investigation. He pleaded not guilty, and the case was later dropped when Trump returned to office.

Harp and Nauta were among a small group of aides who accompanied Trump into a catering truck as he secretly switched planes in Turkiye in July, amid reported threats to his safety.

Reporters, staff and figures like Secretary of State Marco Rubio remained on the plane Trump was meant to be on board, which critics have described as a “decoy flight” in case of attack.

articles.title: Pro-Israel Democrat John Fetterman makes video appearance at GOP convention
articles.summary: Pennsylvania senator who has clashed with party over Israel support says he will reject ‘the extremes and socialism’.
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman, a Democrat who has distanced himself from his party, has appeared in a video recording on the first day of the Republican Party’s two-day midterm conventio n in the United States.

The video on Wednesday was a surprise for those who attended the conservative gathering in Dallas, Texas, where President Donald Trump is seeking to galvanise support ahead of the November elections.

“Yes, I’m Senator John Fetterman, Pennsylvania. Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a common-sense Democrat,” Fetterman said as he introduced his Republican colleague, Senator Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania.

Fetterman, a 57-year-old first-term senator, has cast himself as an outsider within the Democratic Party.

He has offered outspoken support for Israel and the war on Iran , even as voters and progressive voices in his party criticise those elements of US foreign policy.

“I’m always going to stand with America. I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Fetterman said in the video clip.

But his appearance at the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention is likely to exacerbate criticism from his Democratic colleagues.

US Representative Brendan Boyle, another Pennsylvania Democrat, has repeatedly questioned Fetterman’s party allegiance, as well as his commitment to public service. He renewed that sentiment after Wednesday’s video aired.

“A year ago I labeled John Fetterman ‘Trump’s favorite Democrat.’ Tonight, he yet again proves why,” Boyle wrote on social media.

Fetterman has also faced questions about his fitness for office following a series of reports that detail his apparent lack of enthusiasm for his Senate responsibilities.

A recent Wall Street Journal article found that the senator had cancelled meetings with constituents.

In one case, The Wall Street Journal said he skipped a June meeting with injured military veterans, citing illness, only to show up later for a Fox News interview about Israel and its joint war with the US on Iran.

His approval rating is now higher among Republicans in Pennsylvania than among members of his own party.

Last month, a poll from The New York Times, Siena College and The Philadelphia Inquirer suggested that 73 percent of Pennsylvania Republicans approved of Fetterman’s performance, up from 25 percent in 2024.

Meanwhile, Democratic support in the state had slid dramatically over the last two years, slipping from 74 percent to 22 percent. Some 63 percent of Democratic respondents held an unfavourable view of him.

While Fetterman has depicted himself as a maverick within the Democratic Party, he has denied that he would switch parties to become a Republican.

“I’m not going to be a Republican, but I’m going to be a Democrat that’s going to have a conversation with whoever is playing it straight,” he said in a recent interview with Fox News.

Still, speculation about Fetterman’s party credentials has continued as the midterms near.

The election on November 3 will decide which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s term.

Republicans currently hold a small majority in the House of Representatives and Senate, but they could face a setback at the polls as voters express frustration over cost of living issues and Trump’s deepening unpopularity.

Still, reclaiming the Senate especially could be an uphill climb for Democrats. Only a third of Senate seats are up for re-election this year, compared with all 435 House seats.

Fetterman is not up for re-election until 2028.

articles.title: George W Bush recalls moment with Derek Jeter before nerve-wracking pitch at Yankee Stadium after 9/11
articles.summary: Former President George W. Bush recalls throwing the ceremonial first pitch at Yankee Stadium weeks after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
articles.body: Former President George W. Bush recalled Wednesday a lighthearted moment he shared with New York Yankees shortstop Derek Jeter before throwing out a ceremonial first pitch at Yankee Stadium just weeks after 9/11. Bush told the story alongside Condoleezza Rice, his national security advisor at the time of the attacks, during a reunification event at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Texas. During the World Series in October 2001, Bush said he was feeling the pressure of leading the nation through a fragile moment when Jeter told him before the game, "Don’t bounce it, they’ll boo you." GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS "I looked at the catcher, he looked really tiny, and the ball felt really heavy," Bush said. While scanning the faces in the crowd, Bush said he could imagine people thinking, "You can knock down our buildings, but you d— sure not going to touch our soul." AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS Bush recalled throwing the ball, which made it over the plate, and described the moment as "memorable." "I mean, it was an amazing feeling," he said. articles.title: Talarico says he 'missed the mark' as he backtracks on controversial woke statements
articles.summary: James Talarico now backs banning transgender surgeries for minors and opposing trans athletes in girls' sports as the Texas Senate race heats up.
articles.body: In a Fox News exclusive interview, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico came out in favor of banning gender surgery for minors and opposed transgender-identifying men competing in women’s sports. Talarico also backtracked on several of his more controversial claims, including saying there are six genders and that "God is nonbinary." This comes as the Texas Senate race, which is surprisingly close according to recent Fox News polling, enters its final months. The race is considered critical to both parties' chances of securing a Senate majority. Talarico is facing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican who has faced controversies of his own. A Republican loss in Texas would significantly impact President Donald Trump's ability to implement his agenda. Fox News spoke with Talarico at a food drive campaign event in Dallas on Tuesday. Talarico’s event took place as the first-ever GOP midterm convention kicked off just miles away in downtown Dallas. TALARICO CAMPAIGNS WITH SURGEON WHO OPERATED ON TRANSGENDER MINORS: ‘WOLF IN SHEEP’S CLOTHING’ Asked whether he would vote as a U.S. senator in favor of a national ban on gender surgery for minors, Talarico answered, "Absolutely." He said, "I've been consistent on this issue," explaining his opposition to a Texas bill to ban transgender surgeries on minors by saying the measure "was overly broad." "If you go back and check, I voted for a major amendment to limit the bill to banning surgeries for minors," he said. "As a lawmaker, my job is to try to sift through everything the bill does. And sometimes there's stuff in it that's really harmful, and I have no choice but to oppose the bill as a whole." "It's why I try to use amendments, to narrow the focus of the bill so that it does exactly what we intend it to do," he continued. "It's what I tried to do with that piece of legislation, and unfortunately the amendment I supported was unsuccessful." In 2023, as a member of the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico voted against a state bill titled SB 14, which prohibited certain gender surgery, puberty blockers and certain hormone treatments for minors. There were 18 amendments to the bill proposed by Democrats, all of which Talarico voted in favor and all of which ultimately failed. In the same interview, Talarico acknowledged that men in women’s sports is a significant issue in Texas. He said, "I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness." "Every sport has to be safe and fair. As a former public school teacher, I care a lot about our student athletes. I care a lot about our students. And so, I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness," he said. Talarico’s comments mark a shift from his earlier position as a Texas state lawmaker. In 2021, while serving on the Texas House Public Education Committee, he opposed SB 29, which sought to require public-school athletes to compete based on the biological sex listed on their birth certificate, calling the issue a "manufactured problem." Later that year, he voted against HB 25, which enacted similar restrictions into Texas law. JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY' He also addressed perhaps his most controversial statement, which he made in 2021, while opposing a Texas bill to keep men out of women’s sports. Talarico said on the state House floor that "God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary." "I was being provocative with that statement. I get that," Talarico admitted, explaining, "What I was trying to say is that you can't use human categories to define God, and that's not controversial theologically. In fact, the late Charlie Kirk, the late Pope Benedict all said the same thing." Talarico continued, claiming "these comments are being clipped out of context to try to distract from Ken Paxton's career of corruption." "You mentioned [Paxton] being acquitted in the state Senate. That was after two of his billionaire megadonors gave the lieutenant governor a $3 million check to buy his acquittal," Talarico said. "So, Ken Paxton is the most corrupt politician in Texas and he's gonna try to clip some of my comments, including comments where I was being a little provocative in order to try to distract from that career." Fox News Digital reached out to the Paxton campaign for a response. LONGTIME GOP AIDE DEFECTS TO DEM RISING STAR AS TEXAS SENATE BATTLE FOR CORNYN'S SEAT HEATS UP Regarding his past comment about there being more than two genders, Talarico said he does not currently believe there are six sexes. "I've missed the mark on some of my past statements. I will be the first to admit it," he said. "What I meant is that there are two sexes, and then there's a small percentage of people with genetic abnormalities." "Obviously didn't say it correctly. There are not six sexes. There are two, and I think the reason that politicians in that convention center across the street want to talk about six sexes is because they don't want to talk about $6 diesel," he said. Though he walked back these controversies, Talarico did not hold back on his criticism of the Supreme Court, which he described as "infected" with corruption, saying it "needs to be overhauled." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER He said that if elected, "You're going to expect that I will vote for overhaul to the Supreme Court. That will include binding codes of conduct for our justices. It'll include term limits, and I am open to a discussion about expanding the number of justices." Following these controversies, Talarico pledged to keep his message focused on affordability for the remainder of the campaign. "Everywhere I go across the state of Texas, people are struggling to survive in this economy. They are struggling to afford the basics: groceries, gas, utilities, healthcare. And that's what I'm going to be focused on from now until Election Day." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On the topic of affordability, Talarico said that "we should not have a state income tax" in Texas. This is despite Talarico previously voting against a measure to permanently ban a state income tax, which he suggested was redundant and an example of "government waste at its worst." The measure was ultimately passed by the Texas Legislature and approved by Texas voters in November 2019.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: 25 years after 9/11, ICE says more than 2K known or suspected terrorists have been deported
articles.summary: ICE arrested over 2,150 known or suspected terrorists and deported more than 2,000 since Trump took office, DHS says ahead of the 9/11 anniversary.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has deported more than 2,000 known or suspected terrorists from the U.S. since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) tells Fox News Digital, as the nation prepares to mark 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks. DHS said ICE arrested more than 2,150 known or suspected terrorists between Jan. 20, 2025, and Sept. 9, 2026, and deported 2,015 during that period. "As we reflect on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the brave men and women of ICE continue to carry out their duty to protect the homeland and keep the American people safe," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the department’s announcement. articles.title: Fetterman teases where his true loyalty lies after surprise appearance at GOP convention
articles.summary: Senate Democrat John Fetterman drew a hard line after introducing Dave McCormick at the Republican National Committee's midterm convention.
articles.body: DALLAS — A rogue Senate Democrat toying with the idea of leaving his party drew a hard line in the sand after making a surprise appearance at the GOP’s Trump-centric convention. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., has been welcomed with open arms by Republicans to join the party after he floated leaving his own caucus, and spurred further speculation that he would jump ship after dropping a video introducing his colleague, Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention on Wednesday. But in a statement to Fox News Digital, the progressive-turned centrist said that he wasn’t turning his back on the Democratic Party, even as the knives have come out to cut him loose from the Senate. DEM SENATOR DELIVERS SURPRISE VIDEO AT REPUBLICAN CONVENTION BACKING MCCORMICK "My remarks introduced Dave McCormick as a great American and friend. We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA," Fetterman said. "We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life." "I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party — and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on," he continued. Fetterman started his career in the Senate after besting Dr. Mehmet Oz in a tight race for power in 2022, where he clinched a historically thin Democratic majority in 2022 running on a progressive platform. TOP REPUBLICAN NAMES WHO HE SAYS IS REALLY LEADING DEMOCRATS — AND IT'S NOT SCHUMER OR JEFFRIES But since then, he has become a thorn in Democrats’ side, and challenged the direction of the party. Earlier this year, Fetterman warned that if Democrats became more entrenched in anti-Israel policy positions, he would exit the party, and has taken jabs at the party’s direction during this midterm election cycle as far-left progressives, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, have emerged as standard-bearers. Fetterman has routinely bucked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his colleagues on a handful of key issues, like President Donald Trump’s war in Iran or voting with Republicans to end the marathon government shutdown last Fall. FETTERMAN FACES DEM REVOLT AS BOMBSHELL REPORT FUELS PUSH TO OUST HIM: 'DISGRACE' His latest edict followed a bombshell report that alleged through leaked texts with his aides that the maverick Democrat would often brush off duties of his office, like meeting with paralyzed veterans or charging that a three-hour funeral service for slain police officers was a "non-starter." And Republicans would gladly welcome him into the fold. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said in July that he and others in the Senate GOP have had "had conversations with him in the past … about the challenges he faces in his caucus." But for now, Fetterman is staying put even if Democrats flip the Senate in November.

articles.title: Trump says the war in Iran will end after Election Day
articles.summary: During his speech at the Republicans’ midterm convention, President Donald Trump reinforced his commitment to ensuring Iran doesn’t possess a nuclear weapon.
articles.body: DALLAS — President Donald Trump tried to turn one of his biggest political vulnerabilities into a strength for Republicans here Wednesday, making the war with Iran a key focus of his speech at the party’s midterm convention. “Does anybody here think that Iran should have a nuclear weapon? Anybody?” Trump asked the crowd at American Airlines Center, articulating the administration’s core argument for attacking Iran. The audience responded loudly and decisively: “No!” Trump also repeated a claim he made to reporters earlier in the day. “The war will be over very shortly after the election,” Trump said. “They’re hanging out for dear life, hoping that we lose, so they can deal with dumb, weak Democrats and they can have their nuclear bomb. But we’re not going to let that happen.” The war Trump once predicted would last only four or five weeks is now in its seventh month. A recent NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey found that 69% of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war. The share of Republicans who say they strongly approve of his handling of the war has dropped 18 percentage points since the spring and now stands at 30%. Several people at the convention who spoke to NBC News said Trump has earned their trust on the war. “Any good thing in life is worth waiting for, and so if you put the Iran war and its ultimate conclusion in that context, I think that puts a slightly different light on it,” said Jack Etheridge, an alternate delegate from Ohio. “I mean, let’s face it: The election is part of the timeline. The Iranians are taking advantage of that, I think, for their own purposes, but I think the reality is no one believes that Iran is going to defeat the United States.” Others echoed Trump’s demand that Iran not develop or possess a nuclear weapon. “They are not just a bad dictatorship like China or Russia. They are an extremist theocratic dictatorship, and they would drop a nuclear bomb on Europe,” said David Lovlien, a county commissioner in Merrimack County, New Hampshire. “We are going to save so many lives doing what we are doing over there versus doing nothing.” Vince Galko, a former top Pennsylvania GOP official, conceded that higher gas prices brought on by the war have stung. “But,” Galko added, “I also think consumers can afford to look at $4 gas for a few weeks rather than looking at a mushroom cloud over their kids’ school.” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said it’s on Trump to explain and sell the war to Americans. “If you explain to people, ‘OK, here’s your choice, would you like us to stop Iran from trying to kill or allow them to kill us?’ I think it’s a good choice. I can defend it,” Scott said. “I think he’s done the right thing.” In his speech Wednesday, Trump predicted that oil and gas prices would come down once the war ends. “You know, it happens to me all the time. Guys come up, you know, ‘I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran; gasoline’s up,’” said Trump, dramatizing a conversation that he said ends with him winning the argument. “Let me ask you one question: Can Iran have a nuclear weapon? Absolutely not! Well, then I’m right — then I win!”

articles.title: Trump tries to energize his base by placing himself front and center: ‘I’m on the ballot’:
articles.summary: President Donald Trump spoke on the first night of the GOP midterm convention, where he promised — without specifics — that Americans would get dividend checks if Republicans keep Congress.
articles.body: DALLAS — President Donald Trump wants to make one thing clear: His name is not on the ballot in November, but his supporters need to vote like it is. Republicans from across the country convened here Wednesday for their party’s first-ever midterm convention, an event designed to put Trump front and center in the closing stages of the midterm election cycle. “Pretend that I am on the ballot,” Trump said to loud cheers during his keynote address Wednesday night. “I’m on the ballot.” Indeed, Trump was the star of the show. Speakers mentioned his name 155 times, and Trump invoked his own name 16 times, bringing the total mentions to 171. The only other word mentioned more was variations of “America.” Trump’s approval ratings are at an all-time low, and the party is worried about MAGA voters’ not turning out in large numbers — historically a problem for Republicans when Trump is not running. Trump tried to energize his base with a speech that was a hallmark of his presidential campaign — lengthy, winding and full of insults directed at his opponents. Trump leaned into the headwinds his party faces, walking the audience through the long-running political dynamic that the party that controls the White House generally struggles during midterms. “The midterms are not supposed to be won by the sitting president,” he said. “We are going to change that.” For much of the first day of the convention, the crowd at American Airlines Center was sparse. Before Trump took the stage, however, the lower sections filled up, and there was noticeably more energy for his speech. The upper sections, however, remained largely empty. Outside of persuading Republicans to vote during the midterms, much of Trump’s speech focused on issues that he regularly talks about at political rallies; he repeatedly mentioned closing the southern border, tax cuts and boosting domestic energy production. “I gave you the biggest tax decreases in the history of our country,” Trump said to loud cheers. “We will have American energy independence. ... We will have energy dominance.” Trump also promised that his administration would hand out $5,000 dividend checks to Americans if Republicans hold on to Congress. “If Republicans win both the House and the Senate, because of our tremendous economic success, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States for $5,000,” he said, adding that the money would have to be spent in the U.S. Trump did not specify where the money would come from or how he would enforce where it was spent. Trump has made similar promises in the past that went unfulfilled. Shortly after he returned to office, Trump said the so-called Department of Government Efficiency — which was led by billionaire Elon Musk and created chaos and job losses in the federal government — would pass its savings on to the public. Those checks never materialized. He also floated giving Americans dividends from tariff revenue, which also has not happened. NBC News reached out to the White House about where the administration would get the roughly $1.35 trillion Trump’s idea would cost — or how the requirement to spend it in the U.S. would be enforced. The backdrop of the convention is an election cycle in which Republicans are trying to hold on to slim majorities in both the House and the Senate. Democrats have been optimistic that they can retake the House, and the next Senate majority will run through a handful of key states that have been flooded with money from both parties. This week, a Trump-aligned super PAC spent nearly $50 million on ad buys in seven Senate races. The largest chunk, $14 million, went to back Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who is running in Michigan’s Senate race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a young, progressive, Muslim candidate whom Republicans nationally have cast as a villain in their effort to paint Democratic candidates across the country as too far to the left. “Mike Rogers, your candidate over there, is a wonderful man,” Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee, said in his speech Wednesday night. “But he faces a dangerous, radical and weird Abdul El-Sayed.” The comment drew the largest round of boos from the crowd in the early evening part of the event. The Trump-aligned super PAC ad buy also included $12 million in Ohio, where Republican Sen. Jon Husted is running against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said he thinks Republicans will hold the Senate but acknowledged that in states like Georgia, where Republican Rep. Mike Collins is trying to oust well-funded Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, the party faces some challenges. “Mike Collins doesn’t have as much money, so it makes it harder,” Scott said. “It’s hard beating incumbents.” Texas, the host state for the convention, also features a competitive race with scandal-plagued Texas Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton running against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico. Trump called Paxton the “greatest” attorney general in Texas history and urged people to make sure he gets elected — but not before he joked about how Paxton talks and dresses. “You may not like the way he looks, but in the history of Texas, he is the single greatest attorney general you have ever had,” Trump said. Trump also spent a chunk of time going after Talarico, claiming he is against eating meat — which Talarico has denied — and calling him “weird-looking.” Trump said roughly 35 seats in both the House and the Senate are considered tossups, and he pledged to hold events in all of those races. “The ones that are very close, they might be winning by a little or losing by a little or tied,” Trump said. “I am going to go to every one of those states.” As the convention opened, floor operations staff members circulated placards for people to wave with the names of candidates who took the stage, bringing a broader purpose to an event designed mainly around Trump. When Texas congressional candidate Carlos De La Cruz and his sister, U.S. Rep. Monica De La Cruz, spoke, delegates from all states waved the signs bearing their names. “We’re here to promote our party, and this brings attention to it,” said Charles Pritchard, an Arkansas delegate who sat alone in a largely empty last row during the program’s first hour. “You’re from NBC. You might not be here otherwise.” Rachel Ruffer, an Ohio delegate, looked on the bright side of low attendance. “It’s a smaller crowd, so it’s actually very nice and easy to get around and everything,” she said. Some state Republican parties across the country grumbled about the hastily planned midterm convention, as NBC News reported last week. One of the biggest concerns was that it comes so close to Election Day, which forces candidates who want to attend to take precious time away from the campaign trail. Several House members in competitive races are skipping the event to focus on their campaigns. Organizers, though, said the timing was intentional, because so-called low-propensity voters, who do not regularly vote in midterm elections, really begin paying close attention to campaigns only after Labor Day. Concerns also linger about Trump’s historically low approval ratings and whether it helps or hurts the party to make him the focus of its midterm strategy. The war in Iran, now over six months old, remains highly unpopular, and the Trump administration has struggled to bring down rising costs, including an increase in the price of fuel that is directly related to the war. “I’m kind of glad Trump is going against an NFL game,” said a Republican strategist in attendance, referring to the fact that the start of the midterm convention coincides with the start of the professional football season. “It means fewer people will be watching.” Jack Etheridge, an alternate delegate from Ohio, acknowledged “challenges” in Trump’s second term but rated his performance highly overall. “What I’m seeing is that President Trump is working in the toughest job in the world right now,” Etheridge said as he charged his phone in the arena’s concourse. “I’ve made some mistakes in my life, so I have to be careful about saying, ‘Well, he should have done this, should have done that.’ I feel like he’s rising to the occasion. You know, he’s indefatigable.” The mood on the main stage was heavily positive, focusing on Trump’s first two years in office, as speakers said he has drastically reduced the flow of undocumented immigrants through the southern border and touted his biggest legislative achievement, the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill, which included removing taxes on tips and Social Security. Those policies have become mainstays in Republicans’ midterm messaging. Democrats have regularly pointed out that the bill disproportionately benefited wealthy Americans. The scaled-down convention did include traditional parties and political fundraisers, many of which dotted downtown Dallas on Tuesday evening. An event at the downtown eatery The Rustic was one of the main events, featuring a handful of Trump political aides, including Chris LaCivita, and Rep. Byron Donalds, the Trump-backed Florida gubernatorial candidate, hosted an event at the House of Blues. Among the speakers at that event was Collins, the Georgia Senate candidate, who joked with the audience that he wanted to say “Go Dawgs,” a reference to the University of Georgia football team, a top rival of the University of Florida. One day later on the convention’s main stage, Trump made sure that the reason for the unprecedented midterm GOP convention was crystal clear. “When I’m on the ticket, Republicans always do very well,” he said. “We won it big, and we also won everything else.”

articles.title: Fetterman says he’ll still caucus with Democrats after video appearance at GOP midterm convention
articles.summary: Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) confirmed Wednesday night he still plans to caucus with the Democratic Party despite making a video appearance during the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention. “My remarks introduced Dave McCormick as a great American and friend. We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA,” Fetterman said in a statement…
articles.body:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) confirmed Wednesday night he still plans to caucus with the Democratic Party despite making a video appearance during the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention.

“My remarks introduced Dave McCormick as a great American and friend. We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA,” Fetterman said in a statement released after his prerecorded remarks aired. “We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life.”

He continued, “I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party—and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”

Fetterman, not mentioned in the event’s agenda, introduced via video fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick (R) — who spoke in person during the Dallas convention’s first night. The Democrat praised his GOP counterpart in the recording, which played on all screens in the American Airlines Center.

“David McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done,” Fetterman said in the video said, highlighting their joint efforts to revitalize Pennsylvania’s manufacturing industry — an effort President Trump also backed.

The Democrat went on to call McCormick a “great friend.” Fetterman has built a close relationship with his fellow Pennsylvania senator; the two launched a joint political action committee, Common Ground PA, in July — seeking to target donors who support both lawmakers.

Fetterman has attracted the ire of his Democratic colleagues in both chambers for repeatedly breaking with the party. In July, the Democrat was the only member of his party to vote against a war powers resolution seeking to force Trump to wind down the Iran war.

Just days before this vote, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) had pledged to welcome Fetterman to the Republican Party, adding that he and other GOP colleagues had already approached the Pennsylvania Democrat about the idea.

Earlier that summer, Fetterman said at the Hill Nation Summit that he would leave the Democratic Party if it turned its back on Israel entirely.

A late August New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University poll of registered voters in Pennsylvania found that a higher percentage of Republicans — 73 percent — had a favorable opinion of Fetterman compared to Democrats, with 22 percent.

Fetterman also polled higher than Pennsylvania’s GOP senator among Republican respondents, with only 63 percent viewing McCormick favorably.
