articles.body:
President Trump renewed his calls on Wednesday for Republicans to pretend that he’s on the ballot in November, promising $5,000 for every U.S. adult if the GOP holds onto the House and Senate.

“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said in the keynote address at the RNC midterm convention in Dallas. “Just one more time, because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts. You’re going to lose your safety and security. You’re going to lose your wealth.”

The president has begun to urge Republicans to vote as if his name will be on the ballot in recent weeks amid a tough election landscape, with the GOP grappling with historical headwinds, Trump’s sinking approval ratings and fallout from the war in Iran.

“The midterms are not supposed to be won by the sitting president, and we’re going to change that, and we’ll make it an even more important time in our country and presidency,” he continued, noting it’s a “beautiful challenge”

In an effort to boost turnout for GOP candidates, Trump pledged to disburse “Trump dividends” of $5,000 if Republicans hang onto their slim majorities in the House and Senate.

He noted Wednesday that the government could issue these payments “because we’ve done so well and because our country is making so much money,” though it’s unclear what legal questions such a move could pose.

He added that the payments could only be used in the U.S. but did not offer any other details.

Throughout his nearly two-hour speech, Trump praised his sweeping tariff agenda and trade deals. He noted that “tariff” was once his “most-favorite word,” but it has since moved to fifth place.

“Trillions of dollars in tariff revenue have come in,” he said. “Record investments from foreign countries and enormous new equity stakes in major companies.”

The president also repeated his pledge to hit the campaign trail for Republican candidates in battleground races ahead of the general election.

“We can win every one of those races, but I’m going to go to every one of those states for congressmen and for senators,” he said. “I’m going to do that, and we’re going to have rallies.”

He also spoke about the Iran war, telling Tehran “not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard.”

He said people come up to him “all the time” and say they wished he hadn’t started the Iran war, which has become increasingly unpopular among voters.

“I say … ‘Let me ask you one question: Can Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ ‘Absolutely not,’” he said. “Well, then I’m right that I went in.”

He repeated his predictions that oil prices will tick down when the conflict concludes, noting this will be after the Nov. 3 elections.

“The war will be over very shortly after the election,” he said. “They’re hanging out for dear life, hoping that we lose, so they can deal with dumb, weak Democrats, and they can have their nuclear bomb.”

Trump received cheers from the crowd over his executive order to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” He also talked about changing the name of the Strait of Hormuz to the “Trump Strait.”

Nearly half-way through his lengthy speech, the president joked that he loves to “weave” between different issues in his remarks.

“I love ‘the weave,’ you know what ‘the weave’ is,” he said. “You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom, or you bring in an airplane, or you bring in Air Force One, but you notice I always get right back to the same topic.”

“Someday there’ll be a time when I don’t get back to the original subject, and then you can say, ‘He’s had it,’ OK?”

He only spoke briefly about his renovations at the White House as well as the new Air Force One plane.

articles.summary: DALLAS — The Republican National Committee’s first-ever midterm convention lived up to its “Trump-a-palooza” nickname as the two-day Dallas bash kicked off Wednesday. articles.body:
DALLAS — The Republican National Committee’s first-ever midterm convention lived up to its “Trump-a-palooza” nickname as the two-day Dallas bash kicked off Wednesday.

Posters of the president — from Oval Office meetings to his triumphant stance in Butler, Pa., — dotted the American Airlines Center’s walls. Red, white and blue baseball caps emblazoned with Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan were for sale at the convention’s merch stop. And attendees from Texas and beyond were quick to say that the president was their main reason for showing up.

“Trump,” said Amy Osterman, an Illinoisan attending her first party convention, when asked what she was looking forward to about the program. “I’m just excited to get reenergized for the midterms. Like, let’s go. We need to do this.”

The outsized focus on Trump, who is not on the ballot this fall, comes as some Republicans admit to mixed feelings about whether vulnerable candidates should align themselves so closely with the president amid his lackluster approval numbers, with some battleground lawmakers steering clear of the Lone Star State.

“In actuality, I really am running. We don’t really know it but we are. I mean, we’re running together,” Trump said as he capped off the convention’s first night. “We have to have Congress. We have to have the majorities. If we don’t have the majorities, so much can be lost.”

The president implored Republicans to “pretend that I’m on the ballot,” and went on to offer up a $5,000 dividend incentive to every American adult if his party keeps Democrats from taking back the House this fall. He called them “Trump dividends” and said they had to be spent in the U.S.

Fifty-five days out from the election, Trump and other Republicans leaned in heavily on messaging that a blue wave election would wreak havoc on the president’s record and prevent the GOP from moving forward on his “America First” priorities.

“If we hand America’s future to the radical left Democrats … our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet,” Trump said, adding that this “would be a tragedy.”

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said that the “ideals of 1776” are “under threat” from Democrats, claiming the party would reopen the border “immediately” if they returned to power.

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) blasted Democrats over recent primary successes from progressive Democrats, some of whom are members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

“To the American people listening, I say, if all you want out of life is what little these communists are offering, I guess that’s your right. Or you can join Donald J. Trump and Republicans, and have the opportunity to realize your greatest dreams,” Emmer said.

Other top Republican figures ripped their Democratic rivals as “dangerous.”

One Democrat even made a surprise appearance at the convention Wednesday, ripping the party’s shift to the left.

“I’m always going to reject the extremes in socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Sen. John Fetterman said in a prerecorded video introducing his Republican colleague Sen. Dave McCormick to the convention stage.

The convention, the first held by a major party outside of a presidential election year, comes amid as the GOP’s midterm outlook grows increasingly bleak .

In analysis last week, Cook Political Report suggested that Republicans’ “nightmare scenario” had now become the most likely midterm landscape. Decision Desk HQ now forecasts that the House leans in favor of Democrats — and, while the Senate is close to a coin toss, Democrats are narrowly favored in the upper chamber, too.

DDHQs latest polling average shows Trump’s approval rating is roughly 18 percentage points underwater, with just 39 percent giving his job handling a thumbs-up. Democrats also have a 7-point advantage on a generic congressional ballot.

Against that backdrop, Republicans are hopeful that the convention will excite their base and drive turnout in the fall.

But others have signaled the optics of the so-called convention aren’t ideal as vulnerable candidates navigate voter frustration over Trump’s moves on the economy, the war in Iran and more.

A Politico survey of more than 70 Republican candidates and lawmakers last week found that more than half planned to skip the event. Some of the most at-risk Republicans this year, including Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), are expected to be absent.

As he addressed the crowd, Trump described the arena as “packed,” pushing back on characterizations of a small crowd — though swathes of seats and suites, which can hold some 20,000 attendees, appeared sparse following concerns about the timing and attraction of the convention. T he Hill has reached out to the RNC for attendance figures.

Still, more than a dozen attendees told The Hill that Trump was the biggest draw.

Steve Novak, who went to the 2024 convention in Milwaukee, traveled from Minnesota for the president’s pair of speeches. Rosie Swanson, a Texan attending her first Republican convention, said she “would’ve come from anywhere” to see the president at the event.

Elsewhere in Dallas, Democrats embraced the convention as their own political opportunity, with counterprogramming from House Democrats, Texas Senate hopeful James Talarico and more.

Talarico, who’s ahead of Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in recent polling of the Senate race, took part in a media blitz alongside a statewide “Love Thy Neighbor” food drive. He described the convention as Republicans “toasting to their own corruption,” as reported by the Associated Press.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate who recently launched a new PAC aimed at helping elect Democrats. stopped in Texas on Wednesday, hammering Vice President Vance, Trump’s 2028 heir apparent. He also called the convention “bizzare.”

Multiple progressive groups, labor unions and others — including Next Generation Action Network, Powered by the People, Texas Democrats and the AFL-CIO — are planning demonstrations in Dallas on Thursday, when Vance will address the crowd and Trump will give a second speech.

Mallory Wilson contributed to this report.
